g1-emuA.text: Limitations of Existing Online Resources on Psychedelics Most of the writing online about psychedelics feels outdated, primarily because psychedelics are being regulated now in so many places. Licensed psilocybin service centers opened in Oregon in 2023. In 2025, Colorado implemented a regulated system for natural medicines and began the licensing process, and New Mexico passed a Medical Psilocybin Act also in 2025. In Australia, since 2023, psychiatrists working in certain settings have been able to access psilocybin and MDMA for a specific list of conditions.

g1-emuB.text: Problem is most writing in this space is out of date as soon as it’s written. Here are a few rapidly-emerging trends relevant to communities: Legal retail psilocybin services spaces are now open in Oregon and will be legal in Colorado (beginning in 2025) under a different, but equally robust regulatory system for natural medicines. New Mexico has also recently enacted its Medical Psilocybin Act which will also begin licensing in 2025. Since 2023, in Australia, psychiatrists can access psilocybin and MDMA for a narrow range of conditions.

g2-emuA.text:
It does also attract people who are all for revelution but not so much for working, having 12 revelutions and 6 stories of where you come from but still can't say sorry to your housemate. When your running a community based around revelution these things will come up and need to be dealt with. Sometimes the dishes need doing and a scared kid needs comforting.

My own experience tends to show that there are some good reasons for the communal use of Psychedelics. One being that they lower defences and the other that they are a great way of building a strong bond between a group of people by experiencing some of the harder times that come up when people take the medicine. As you point out though there are some negative aspects that can come from taking psychedelics, among them being confusion, grandiosity, dependency, and a few ways that they can foul up the dynamics between people. The question is are you mature enough as a community to be able to pick through the good and the bad?

g2-emuB.text:
It does draw a lot of people who want revelation but don't want to do the work, though, and if you're forming a community primarily around getting a peak experience, you're going to find a lot of people who are going to have trouble doing the ordinary work of living together.

But I think that you make a very good point about communal use. I think that it can be very helpful to have the defenses that psychedelics break down when you're trying to have a deep conversation. And I think it can be a very bonding experience to go through a tough medicine night together. It can also make people confused, grandiose, dependent, and it can be very confusing in terms of relationships between people. The question is whether or not the community can mature to a point where it can distinguish the good from the bad.

g3-emuA.text:
Also your peers can help reality check any downloads you may have had. Psychedelics can create a lot of nonsense as well as insight, and on the spot they often feel very similar. Having a few friends that know your history can help you sort out what’s actually useful from what’s just… mom showing up again.

They can help you time your ceremonies. A lot of traditional medicines rely on a community to help time ceremonies, which can be a great help to get off of the compulsive cycle of taking the medicine and allow you to spend more time integrating.

g3-emuB.text:
This will help you keep the content grounded in reality, and get an idea of how much of what you downloaded is nonsense, caused by the psychedelics. It's very hard to tell what is real insight and what is nonsense on psychedelics, it can all seem equally meaningful and valid. Friends who know your past might be able to tell which insights are new and which are just something you've believed for a while.

As many traditional systems of medicine use set, communal ceremony times for people to partake in ceremony, it will help you not fall into the trap of doing it compulsively, and give you enough time to integrate.

g4-emuA.text: There are no special shamans. This statement is often contested by traditional lineages who point out that many ayahuasca and Bwiti communities revere the authority of particular lineages to be the only ones fit to dispense these medicines. I must concede that there is much I have learned from these traditions.

g4-emuB.text: There will be no ‘shamans’ here. I know this will upset a lot of the traditional lineage people, many of whom I have learnt from in my use of Ayahuasca and Bwiti.

g5-emuA.text: I agree that even in a culture of peer medicine, there would still be an informal "shaman", someone who everyone trusts and isn't questioned. I don't know if it would be possible to avoid this. Things that might help would be to have rotation of roles, and to make everyone publicly accountable for what they do. Though neither of these seem like a complete solution.

g5-emuB.text: It occurs to me that even in a culture of peer-led medicine, there could still be someone who becomes the shaman in the sense of being someone that people trust more and don't question, even if they don't take on that role themselves. I'm not sure if this is something that can or needs to be avoided, but ways to mitigate it would include having people rotate through the role and making sure that they are accountable to the people they are helping in some public way. Neither of these seems like a panacea to me.

g6-emuA.text: This doesn't mean that peer led is casual. It means that more competence is required to lead the group. Screening for medical or psychiatric contraindications and reviewing medications and combinations is a must. An appropriate sober sitter is required. In addition, it will be necessary to decide what should be dealt with by seeking professional medical or psychiatric help or going to the emergency room.

g6-emuB.text: This does not mean that peer-led means casual. When one is removing the hierarchy of authority, one needs to be even more competent. This includes screening for medical and psychiatric reasons that make taking the medication ill-advised, understanding the medication and how it may interact with other medications, making sure the person has the right kind of sober sitter, and agreeing ahead of time about what will require professional or emergency care.

g7-emuA.text:
The reason is that medicine is a secondary thing, which comes after having addressed the most basic things: reparenting/somatic capacity and also working with your peers (the counseling thing). It is meant to improve upon something you already have. You can’t, by decree (and what the medicine does is essentially a decree), grant someone months of real relationship they haven’t had.

This also prevents experience collectors from getting into the way. What’s the likelihood that someone who won’t do six months of this kind of relationship work is going to magically do it after having some visions?

Another thing is that your integration is, well, your life. If anything from the ceremony had effect on you, it will be in your relationships, in your life. You can look at that and see if there has been any change. You can also look at how well you can tolerate frustration.

g7-emuB.text:
One of the reasons the medicine is last in a pl/ork is because there are things that are more fundamental than it, like reparenting, developing somatic capacity, and working with each other. Medicine certainly could enhance that work, but you can't pharmacologically short circuit months of relationship work.

Also, this requirement will weed out the experience collectors.

The 'integration' is normal life. You could see if the ceremony had an effect by asking yourself if you've changed in the slightest way, particularly in relationships and daily behavior. Also, how well are you tolerating frustration?
